spatial_claims.claim: Planes alpha and beta are each perpendicular to plane Pi; their common section is line s; a = alpha ∩ Pi and b = beta ∩ Pi are straight lines
Point A is chosen on s; line p is constructed in alpha through A perpendicular to a; line q is constructed in beta through A perpendicular to b
Case analysis: if A lies in Pi then A lies on both a and b (perpendiculars erected at A); if A not in Pi then perpendiculars dropped from A
p is perpendicular to Pi (by Def. 11.4 applied to alpha ⊥ Pi with p ⊥ a in alpha)
q is perpendicular to Pi (by Def. 11.4 applied to beta ⊥ Pi with q ⊥ b in beta)
p and q both pass through A and are both perpendicular to Pi; if distinct they would be parallel by 11.6, contradicting that they share point A
p and q coincide (they are the same line)
The coincident line p=q lies in both alpha and beta, hence is their common section s by 11.3
s is perpendicular to Pi (since s = p = q and p ⊥ Pi from Step 3)

configuration_map: Plane Pi is the fixed reference plane. Planes alpha and beta are both perpendicular to Pi and intersect each other along line s. The traces a = alpha ∩ Pi and b = beta ∩ Pi are lines in Pi. Point A is chosen on s (hence in both alpha and beta). Line p is constructed in alpha through A perpendicular to a; line q is constructed in beta through A perpendicular to b. By Def. 11.4, both p and q are perpendicular to Pi. By 11.6, since p and q are both perpendicular to Pi and share point A, they must coincide. The coincident line lies in both alpha and beta, so by 11.3 it is s. Therefore s is perpendicular to Pi.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. The proof uses a direct argument (11.6 for parallelism of perpendiculars plus Def. 1.23 to force coincidence) rather than Heath's proof by contradiction (11.13). Every perpendicularity claim follows correctly from Def. 11.4, the identification of lines via 11.6 and 11.3 is valid, and no angle decomposition or interior/exterior point issues arise in this solid geometry perpendicularity argument.
